content: The presence of non-medical staff and peer counselors was highly valued by individuals accessing services. Médicos del Mundo (MdM) is an independent humanitarian organization that provides both emergency and long-term psychosocial support, as well as clinical care, to vulnerable populations. Since 2003, MdM has been conducting traditional HIV testing, and since 2007, it has offered rapid diagnostic testing. These services are available at branch locations in various cities across Spain, primarily targeting socially excluded individuals at high risk of HIV infection, such as sex workers, drug users, and undocumented migrants. MdM emphasizes the use of services provided by the National Health System (NHS) to deliver information and HIV testing services (HTS). For those hesitant to use public healthcare, MdM either accompanies them to NHS facilities or offers testing within its branch offices. Free rapid HIV tests, using fingerstick whole blood or oral fluid, are conducted alongside preand post-test counseling. These services are delivered by a multidisciplinary team, including supervised lay providers trained according to WHO guidelines. Individuals with reactive HIV test results are referred to public hospital HIV/AIDS units for confirmatory testing. Those diagnosed as HIV-positive are linked to treatment and care. For undocumented migrants, MdM provides guidance and support to help them access NHS benefits. Confidentiality of testing and results is strictly maintained, adhering to Spain’s data protection laws. Between 2008 and 2012, MdM tested 3,251 individuals, including 2,253 women, 897 men, and 101 transgender individuals. Of these, 72 new HIV diagnoses were confirmed by public hospitals. The program’s success is attributed to its accessibility, offering free services without requiring appointments or personal identification, which complements traditional NHS HIV testing programs. In India, HIV testing facilities screen clients for symptoms suggestive of tuberculosis (TB) as part of pre-test counseling. Symptomatic patients are systematically referred for further investigations. This activity is routinely reported at district, state, and national levels. Since 2005, Médecins du Monde (MdM) has implemented a harm-reduction program in Yangon, Myanmar, targeting populations at high risk of HIV, including female sex workers, men who have sex with men (MSM), and transgender individuals. The program, developed in collaboration with affected populations, offers comprehensive services such as health education, condom distribution, HTS, STI testing and treatment, HIV care, antiretroviral therapy (ART), and psychosocial support. Peer-led outreach enables the program to reach high-risk populations in settings like brothels and nightclubs. Drop-in centers provide medical care, recreational activities, and social support in a non-discriminatory environment. In 2014, 668 female sex workers and 637 MSM accessed HTS at the Yangon center, with 19% and 30%, respectively, testing HIV-positive. ART retention rates are high, with 85% of female sex workers and 90% of MSM remaining in care after 24 months. In Cambodia, the Cambodian Women for Peace and Development (CWPD) implemented HTS in urban areas, targeting women working in entertainment establishments. Peer providers, trained by the National Center for HIV/AIDS, Dermatology, and STDs, offer rapid HIV and syphilis testing, condoms, and referrals. In 2014, 52% of entertainment workers at the Battambang site received HIV testing, with seven individuals diagnosed as HIV-positive and linked to care. In Chengdu, China, the 1+N community-based HTS program focuses on MSM. Since 2007, collaboration with local Centers for Disease Control (CDC) has enabled the provision of high-quality HTS, including rapid HIV testing, counseling, and linkage to care. Peer counselors conduct anonymous testing in convenient locations, reducing stigma and discrimination. The program has expanded to mobile HTS in gay saunas and escort services. By 2014, the program had provided HTS to 18,683 MSM, diagnosing approximately 250 HIV-positive cases annually and retaining 85% in care for over a year. In Cebu City, Philippines, Transgender COLORS Inc. works to reduce stigma and improve access to HIV services for transgender individuals. Peer educators provide HTS and conduct educational sessions in local communities. From March to June 2014, 508 transgender women were reached, with 7% diagnosed as HIV-positive and linked to care. Client satisfaction surveys revealed a 99% satisfaction rate with the services provided. In Vietnam, the decentralization of HTS to commune health stations (CHS) has improved access in remote areas. A pilot community-based HTS program in Thanh Hoa and Thai Nguyen provinces targeted people who inject drugs and their partners. Outreach teams, including CHS staff and peer educators, provided rapid HIV testing and linked individuals with reactive results to confirmatory testing and care. The program demonstrated a four-fold higher positivity rate compared to facility-based testing, highlighting the feasibility and efficiency of community-based HTS. Globally, innovative programs are being developed to address the needs of populations affected by HIV. These interventions are tailored to overcome social, legal, and logistical challenges, ensuring increased access to HIV testing and care. The examples presented demonstrate leadership in HTS delivery, encouraging collaboration and knowledge-sharing to improve global HIV testing efforts.
